flawed_step: Step 1, the claim that every input gives an O(n log n) comparison count, cannot be justified. The partition sizes depend on where the pivot falls. With the first element as pivot, nothing keeps the split balanced. On a sorted subarray the pivot is the minimum, so the split is 0 and m-1. The recursion depth is then n and the cost is quadratic. The 'no swaps' remark does not help, because running time here is measured in comparisons, not swaps.
counterexample: For each n, take the sorted array [1, 2, ..., n]. On a sorted subarray of length m, the first element is the minimum. Lomuto partition compares every other element with the pivot, which is m-1 comparisons, and none of them is smaller. The result is an empty left part and a sorted right part of length m-1. Adding up, the total is (n-1)+(n-2)+...+1 = n(n-1)/2 comparisons. That is Θ(n²), not O(n log n).
assessment_summary: The statement is false. Deterministic first-element-pivot quicksort with Lomuto partition always uses m-1 comparisons to partition a subarray of length m. On a sorted input, every pivot is the minimum, so each call only shrinks the problem by one. That gives n(n-1)/2 comparisons, which is quadratic. So sorted arrays are the worst case, not a cheap one, and the claimed O(n log n) bound on every input fails.
